newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Nations scrambling to complete plans on Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: Nations scrambling to complete plans on Zaire force.

text.p: With the United Nations close to approving an international force for eastern Zaire, officials on Thursday were scrambling to complete plans that would get troops to the region quickly to feed over a million refugees.

Still not settled, according to diplomats and military advisers, were which troops would go where, how they would eventually leave the region and precisely which air or land routes the contingents would use to reach eastern Zaire.

Canada, which will take the lead in the operation, was expected to write a letter to the U.N. Security Council on Thursday outlining the concept for the force. The operation will be commanded by Lt.-Gen. Maurice Baril, who is conducting a series of meetings with troop contributers.

On hand for the sessions will be White House National Security Adviser Anthony Lake, Defence Undersecretary Walter Slocombe and Air Force Lt. Gen. Peter Pace, who is director of operations for the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
But the 15-member Security Council was not expected to endorse the force before Friday, depending on whether members such as the United States were satisfied with the plans.

About 1.5 million refugees, mainly Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The eastern Zairean province of Kivu has remained politically tense since then, with a new war breaking out in September between Tutsi residents of Zaire and local Zairians backed by Zaire's rag-tag army.

Washington has already sent political and military assessment teams to neighbouring Rwanda and Ottawa intended to send a 24-member military reconnaisance team to eastern Zaire that would leave on Thursday, the Canadian Press reported.

At least 10,000 foreign troops eventually were expected in the region but the initial force would include soldiers from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal, diplomats said. Other African nations have volunteered but needed to wait for funds or transport. Argentina, Brazil and Sweden might also join later.

The international force would remain no longer than six months after which some troops may stay on under a U.N. peacekeeping umbrella. The current operation was being organised outside of the United Nations but endorsed by it.
But there were signs already that the force would meet resistance as relief teams, including those from the U.S. Agency for International Development, have been turned back by rebels.
"This is where the United States has to use its considerable influence with Rwanda and France with Zaire," said one envoy.

Unclear also was how feeding centres would be organised for the refugees without duplicating the current camps, used for bases by the former Hutu army chased out of Rwanda when the Tutsis two years ago took control of the government.

The intention was to set up centres in new areas where anyone carrying weapons would not be allowed to enter. But at the same time the United States and others have declared forcefully that they do not intend to get involved in disarming militia.
"This operation by its very nature is a humanitarian one and the international community is not going in to start a war," said U.N. spokesman Ahmad Fawzi.

"They are going to go in there and try and separate the militia from the real refugees. When you come to be fed you don't need a gun," he said. "Some very useful ideas have been put forward on how to achieve separation without confrontation."
American forces intend to secure the airfield in Goma, Zaire, as well as a three-mile (4.8 km) corridor from Goma to the Rwandan border in an effort to encourage the refugees to return home.

To counter fears of arrests and endless imprisonment into Rwanda's dismal and overcrowded jails, loose plans have been formulated to increase substantially U.N. human rights observers in Rwanda, now numbering only 110 people. Other inducements would include a package of aid for entire communities, including food, medicine, seeds and other necessities, diplomats said.
